description: Recon Village at DEF CON 25 covers reconnaissance and OSINT techniques for information gathering, asset discovery, and attack surface mapping. The 15 talks explore social media analysis, domain discovery, source code research, and practical OSINT methodologies.

talks.title: DFIR Automation Orchestration Tools For OSINT Recon
talks.teaser: Automate OSINT reconnaissance and digital forensics through orchestration tools that streamline attack surface discovery.
talks.summary:
### Bridging the Gap Between DFIR and OSINT
At 00:00, Tyler Rorabaugh takes the stage at the Recon Village to present a practical methodology for modern investigators: applying Digital Forensics and Incident Response (DFIR) automation and orchestration concepts directly to Open Source Intelligence (OSINT). Rorabaugh explains that while corporate security teams have successfully automated incident response playbooks to handle malware alerts, intelligence analysts still conduct OSINT reconnaissance through tedious, manual web searches that hinder investigative scalability.

### The Power of Security Orchestration and Automation (SOAR)
At 04:15 and 09:07, Rorabaugh reviews the emergence of Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response (SOAR) platforms, highlighting tools like Rapid7 Komand, Demisto, and open-source workflow frameworks. He explains how SOAR architectures utilize modular plugins and standardized API connectors to automate sequential workflows—ingesting input indicators, triggering external data lookups, evaluating logical conditions, and formatting structured outputs without human intervention.

### Constructing Automated Reconnaissance Playbooks
At 12:40, the speaker demonstrates constructing an end-to-end automated OSINT pipeline. In his demonstration playbook, an investigator supplies a single target domain name. The orchestration engine automatically executes multiple tasks concurrently: querying DNS servers for subdomains, running WHOIS lookups to identify registrant email addresses, querying certificate transparency logs, checking domain reputation across threat feeds, and executing reverse IP lookups to identify shared hosting infrastructure.

### Integrating Threat Feeds and Social Media Enumeration
At 15:30, Rorabaugh details integrating specialized intelligence sources into orchestration playbooks. He demonstrates pulling passive DNS historical data, querying Shodan for exposed ports and industrial control banners, and automating username searches across social media platforms. By standardizing investigative playbooks, intelligence teams can ensure that every target is subjected to a consistent, comprehensive baseline investigation within seconds.

### Scalable Intelligence Operations and Analyst Empowerment
Concluding between 17:15 and 18:19, Rorabaugh emphasizes that automation does not replace human analytical intuition: rather, it eliminates repetitive data gathering. By automating the mechanical aspects of information gathering, intelligence analysts can dedicate their cognitive energy to complex correlation, behavioral profiling, and strategic decision-making. He encourages researchers to publish open-source automation modules to advance collective OSINT capabilities.

talks.title: Winner Announcement Prize Distribution
talks.teaser: Recognition and prize distribution for contest winners and top performers in the Recon Village.
talks.summary:
### Concluding the DEF CON 25 Recon Village CTF
At 00:03, the organizers of the Recon Village open the closing ceremonies and prize distribution for the inaugural Recon Village Open Source Intelligence (OSINT) Capture The Flag (CTF) competition. The organizers express immense gratitude to the hundreds of participants who competed, noting that the remarkable turnout and competitive energy exceeded all expectations for the village's first official CTF event.

### Celebrating Top Teams and Scoreboard Standings
At 03:40 and 07:50, the organizers display the final competition scoreboard and announce the top-performing teams. They celebrate the podium finishers—including teams "Proprietary Data," "Nosey Parkers," "STFU Darling," and "4815162342"—commending their technical tenacity, analytical precision, and collaborative problem-solving across intense rounds of open-source reconnaissance challenges.

### Reviewing Challenging OSINT Puzzles and Methodology
At 11:15, the presentation recaps the diverse challenge categories designed for the CTF. The organizers review complex scenarios that tested competitors' intelligence-gathering capabilities: geolocating obscure physical landmarks from cropped photographs, tracking hidden operational personas across social media networks, inspecting EXIF metadata and hidden document properties, and identifying concealed indicators across public corporate filings.

### Sponsor Recognition and Prize Distribution
At 14:00 and 15:34, the organizers distribute prizes to the winning teams, presenting hardware gear from Hak5, software-defined radio equipment, specialized commercial training vouchers, and commemorative Recon Village challenge coins. They extend sincere appreciation to the industry sponsors and volunteer infrastructure engineers whose generous support made the competition possible.

### Looking Ahead to Future Recon Village Initiatives
Concluding the ceremony, the village coordinators thank the broader DEF CON community for welcoming the Recon Village into the conference family. They invite participants to provide constructive feedback on challenge design, encourage competitors to author public write-ups of their investigative methodologies, and pledge to expand CTF infrastructure and educational workshops for upcoming DEF CON events.

talks.title: Keynote:  Seeing is Believing   The Future of Recon
talks.teaser: Keynote vision for the evolving landscape of reconnaissance—emerging tools, techniques, and methodologies shaping the future of OSINT.
talks.summary:
### Keynote: The Evolving Landscape of Open Source Intelligence
At 00:00, Shane MacDougall takes the stage to deliver the keynote address for the Recon Village, titled "Seeing is Believing: The Future of Recon." MacDougall surveys the profound evolution of Open Source Intelligence (OSINT) over the preceding decade, tracing its transition from an informal, ad-hoc discipline practiced by hobbyists into an essential, highly scrutinized component of corporate threat intelligence, national security, and investigative journalism.

### The Threat of Data Poisoning and Weaponized Misinformation
At 08:30 and 15:15, MacDougall delivers a warning regarding the vulnerability of public data sources. He explains that as OSINT tools become widely automated, adversaries have begun actively weaponizing data poisoning attacks: seeding public repositories, social media networks, and open-source lists with deliberately falsified indicators, honeypot profiles, and disinformation. Investigators who blindly trust automated tool scrapers risk being manipulated by sophisticated counter-reconnaissance campaigns.

### High-Resolution Geospatial Analysis and Environmental Clues
At 22:42, the speaker demonstrates advanced geolocation techniques using high-resolution commercial satellite imagery, street-level photography, and environmental analysis. He illustrates how expert investigators can pinpoint exact geographic coordinates anywhere on earth by correlating sun angles, shadow lengths, vehicle models, overhead power line configurations, and architectural building styles, proving that visual imagery contains vast layers of forensic evidence beyond immediate pixel content.

### Regulatory Pressures, GDPR, and the Shrinking Open Web
At 31:10 and 37:25, MacDougall analyzes the regulatory headwinds confronting open reconnaissance. The impending enforcement of global privacy legislation, most notably the European Union's GDPR, threatens to redact WHOIS domain registries and restrict public access to corporate ownership records. He explores how the progressive walling-off of social media APIs forces intelligence practitioners to develop resilient, ethical collection methodologies that do not rely on fragile third-party platforms.

### The Ethical Boundaries of Reconnaissance
Concluding between 41:30 and 43:49, MacDougall delivers an impassioned plea regarding the ethics of intelligence gathering. He reminds practitioners that the tools used to uncover malicious cyber actors can easily be repurposed for doxxing, harassment, and corporate espionage. He challenges the audience to uphold strict ethical standards, questioning whether their investigations serve legitimate defensive interests or merely cross into privacy invasion for commercial gain.

talks.title: FERPA: Only Grades Are Safe; OSINT In Higher Education
talks.teaser: Explore OSINT vulnerabilities in higher education systems and how institutions' public data can be exploited to profile students and staff.
talks.summary:
### Higher Education: The Open-Access Security Dilemma
At 00:00, data analyst and researcher Leah Figueroa opens her presentation at the Recon Village by examining the unique cybersecurity posture of higher education. Unlike corporate enterprises that enforce strict network perimeters and data access controls, universities are philosophically designed to be open, collaborative, and publicly accessible environments. Figueroa argues that this open-access culture creates massive reconnaissance opportunities that leave students, faculty, and research data dangerously exposed.

### The Illusory Protection of FERPA
At 05:40 and 11:20, Figueroa deconstructs the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA), the primary federal statute governing student privacy in the United States. She exposes a critical truth: contrary to popular belief, FERPA legally protects only formal academic records—specifically grades, GPA, and transcripts. Non-academic student information is classified as "directory information," which universities can legally publish online unless students actively submit complex opt-out paperwork.

### Harvesting Personal Telemetry from Public University Directories
At 18:20, the speaker demonstrates how easily an adversary can harvest granular student profiles using OSINT techniques. Through public campus directories, student athlete rosters, departmental newsletters, and social media groups, researchers can scrape student home addresses, personal phone numbers, campus employment schedules, dorm locations, and class schedules. Figueroa highlights alarming scenarios where campus health clinics and academic scheduling systems inadvertently leak sensitive personal appointment details.

### Physical Security and Real-World Stalking Risks
At 25:30 and 31:15, the presentation explores the physical safety risks stemming from academic OSINT. Figueroa illustrates how stalkers, abusive ex-partners, or malicious actors can correlate public course schedules with social media check-ins to track students' physical movements across campus in real time. Furthermore, international students and vulnerable populations face heightened risks of state-sponsored harassment and targeted financial fraud enabled by exposed campus directories.

### Reforming Academic Data Policies and Protecting Students
Concluding between 34:10 and 36:39, Figueroa calls for immediate, sweeping reforms in higher education data governance. She urges university administrators to implement privacy-by-default policies, making directory information private unless students explicitly opt in. She advocates for comprehensive privacy awareness training during student orientation, mandatory data minimization across university departments, and regular attack-surface audits to safeguard campus communities.
